title: The new I want
html_source:
In Proteus, Stephen contemplates various characters as models.The narrator says of them, “Houses of decay, mine, his and all. You told the Clongowes gentry you had an uncle a judge and an uncle a general in the army. Come out of them, Stephen. Beauty is not there.”

Phillip M. Weinstein says of these figures, “Each of these identities is a pose, all too common… in an Ireland that is a ‘Paradise of pretenders then and now.” In Nausicaa, Bloom’s thought on this is “The new I want. Nothing new under the sun… Think you’re escaping and run into yourself. Longest way round is the shortest way home.“ In all these examples of escapism, what is realized is that, rebellious as they may be, each carries himself away in the exile, indelibly marked by the very influences he seeks to reject. Weinstein points out: “Nothing new under the sun: sons are born into families, churches, countries… Stephen’s true enemy is sonship itself. He desires to create the world out of himself… Not for nothing does he muse throughout Ulysses over [heresy].” What mature Bloom discovers is that escape is impossible, leaving only acceptance as an option, but an acceptance that leaves him as a “keyless citizen,” which image Joyce imposes on both Bloom and Stephen not just figuratively. What Bloom, partly in his Jewishness, is able to achieve is exile while yet a citizen of Dublin. This has Weinstein, therefore, asserting that, “Ulysses is the greatest celebration of presence in modern fiction. Joyce has created an image of experience in which Yes accommodates No without ceasing to be Yes.
